source.title: Seq vs Seq: An Open Suite of Paired Encoders and Decoders
source.authors: Orion Weller; Kathryn Ricci; Marc Marone; Antoine Chaffin; Dawn J. Lawrie; Benjamin Van Durme

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports downstream benchmark scores across model sizes, bearing conceptually on downstream performance versus scale. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates paired models at several sizes on downstream tasks, but reports no held-out cross-entropy scaling curves, power-law fits, small-run extrapolations, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Mentions of scaling laws and Chinchilla in related discussion are not results from this study. The downstream score series in Table 9 are recorded for V6; other task-specific benchmark comparisons and cross-objective retrieval/MNLI results are not included in the rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains paired encoder and decoder models at six sizes (17M to 1B) with one recipe and reports downstream scores across that size series. These results bear weakly on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6), in a new setting of MLM encoders and cross-objective models. It fits no scaling law, links nothing to pretraining loss, and reports no loss curves. Scaling is not the paper's aim, so this is a weak test of V6 only.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that MLM encoders are better at classification and retrieval and CLM decoders at generative tasks. They add that 50B tokens of continued training on the reverse objective does not close the gap: a 400M encoder beats a 1B decoder on MNLI, and the reverse holds for generative tasks. They make no claims about loss power laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses paired encoder and decoder models with shared data and training recipe, then compares downstream benchmarks across sizes; it does not use the original loss-fitting or compute-allocation methodology.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size and training objective/architecture vary. The 1B runs were trained on 1/3 of the data relative to the intended 2T-token run because compute was unavailable.

fits_no_version.finding: WinoGender accuracy stays near chance (about 50%) for most sizes. It jumps only for native encoders at 400M and 1B (70.3 and 68.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bias or coreference benchmark accuracy is flat, then rises abruptly, with size rather than improving smoothly.

record.problems: No claim-relevant uncertainty estimates or predictive fits are reported for the downstream score series. The 1B models use less training data than intended; the authors state they were scaled to 1/3 of the data. Downstream scores alone do not establish power-law loss scaling or extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: Table 9 also reports cross-objective retrieval and MNLI results (12 rows); excluded to remain within the 60-row limit after retaining the native-model series and cross-objective generative series. Task-level breakdowns in Tables 3, 4, 6, 7, and 8 are not separately recorded; Table 9 supplies the reported aggregate measures used here.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no loss-versus-parameters, tokens or compute curves.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation to larger runs.
No controlled comparison of model shape at fixed parameter count.
No test of the power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.

The 'predictably' part: no fitted relation of downstream score to scale or loss, and no extrapolation. Token count is not held constant (the 1B models saw about 667B tokens versus 2T for the others), so the parameter-only trend is confounded.
No comparison of fitting choices and no evidence that curves bend away from a power law.

record.verdict_notes: This is a weak test of V6. Scores are point evaluations at six sizes, with no uncertainty and no fit. Encoder-task scores come from the best of a fine-tuning sweep. Token budgets differ at 1B, so size is confounded with data. MNLI gains flatten at large sizes (encoder 91.3 to 91.8 from 400M to 1B). The per-task series in Table 8 include some flat or falling points: decoder-from-encoder ARC drops from 22.7 to 20.5 between 17M and 32M, and small models score near zero on TriviaQA. These are declared in rows_left_out. The Table 9 cross-objective retrieval and MNLI series are also declared there.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute curves.
No fits from smaller runs or extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token growth trends.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests of scaling-law form across modalities or the specified alternative training regimes.

Reports downstream scores across six model sizes, but does not fit a predictive relation to scale or pretraining loss, test extrapolation, or report downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No comparison of scaling-law fits or their dependence on fitting choices, nor evidence about power-law bending.

relationships.condition: Native Ettin encoders and decoders, and encoder-from-decoder models, on MS MARCO retrieval, MNLI and the generative average, 17M to 1B
relationships.reason: All three aggregate scores rise monotonically with size (e.g. encoder MNLI 79.5 to 91.8, decoder generative 36.4 to 59.0). The rise is qualitative only; no predictive fit is made (r01-r36, r37, r39, r41, r43, r45, r47).
relationships.display_finding: All three aggregate scores increased monotonically, including encoder MNLI from 79.5 to 91.8 and decoder generative performance from 36.4 to 59.0, without predictive fits.

relationships.condition: Decoder-from-encoder (CLM continued training) models on the generative-task average
relationships.reason: Scores still rise, but the authors say this variant scales poorly with size. Its gap to native decoders grows from near zero at 68M to about 7 points at 1B (r38, r40, r42, r44, r46, r48).
relationships.display_finding: Generative scores rose with size, but the gap to native decoders grew from near zero at 68M to about seven points at 1B.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Native Ettin encoder and decoder models, retrieval, MNLI, and generative-task average across the reported size series
reader_labels.reason: All three reported downstream measures increase across the six sizes for both native architectures (r01-r36).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Cross-objective models on generative-task average across the reported size series
reader_labels.reason: The reported generative average rises across sizes for both encoder-from-decoder and decoder-from-encoder variants, though no predictive fit is tested (r37-r48).
